Lab vs Enzyme Transformations

Which chemical transformations do synthetic chemists and natural enzymes carry out, and how much do the two overlap? Every reaction in two public databases was reduced to its reaction centre, so that the same change on different molecules counts once.

Counts are L1 transformations (defined below) that are robust: seen in at least two independent reactions, or given the same signature by two independent atom mappers. Counts with single sightings include atom-mapping noise.

What counts as a transformation

Each reaction is atom-mapped and reduced to its reaction centre: the atoms whose bonds, hydrogen count, charge or aromaticity change. The rest of the molecule is dropped, so the same change on different substrates is one transformation. How much detail the centre keeps is called the level.

LevelEach centre atom is described bySame transformation, for example
L0element, and the change in hydrogen count and chargealdehyde and ketone reduction
L1element, aromaticity, hydrogen count and charge, before and afterethanal and propanal reduction
L1xas L1, plus the element and aromaticity of each leaving atombromide and iodide leaving groups now differ
L2as L1x, plus the unchanged neighbours of the centre (element, aromaticity, π bonds)aryl and alkyl aldehydes now differ

Four reductions, run through the pipeline

Same letter in a column means the same transformation at that level. Shaded atoms are the reaction centre.

ReactionL0L1L1xL2
ethanal → ethanolAAAA
propanal → propan-1-olAAAA
benzaldehyde → benzyl alcoholAAAB
acetone → propan-2-olABBC
  • L0AC=O → C–O; C +1H; O +1H
  • L1AC=O → C–O; C H1→H2; O H0→H1
  • L1BC=O → C–O; C H0→H1; O H0→H1
  • L2A[C:1]-[CH1:2]=[OH0:3]>>[C:1]-[CH2:2]-[OH1:3]
  • L2B[c:1]-[CH1:2]=[OH0:3]>>[c:1]-[CH2:2]-[OH1:3]
  • L2C[C:1]-[CH0:2](=[OH0:3])-[C:4]>>[C:1]-[CH1:2](-[OH1:3])-[C:4]

At L1, acetone separates from the aldehydes: its carbon goes from no hydrogen to one, while theirs go from one to two. At L2, benzaldehyde separates too, because the carbon next to the centre is aromatic. L1 is the headline level here; every conclusion below holds from L0 to L2.

Two more conventions. Atoms brought in by a reagent are described only as they end up in the product, so the donor is not part of the transformation: methylation by methyl iodide and by S-adenosylmethionine count once, and the donor goes into a separate "how" label. Directions count separately, so a reduction and the matching oxidation are two transformations.

Few shared transformations, but they are the common ones

Share with a precedent on the other side, L1, robust

by distinct transformationsweighted by reactions or records
Table

Labs and enzymes share 702 robust transformations: 43% of the enzymes' and 1.6% of the lab's. Weighted by use, the shares are much higher. 90% of enzyme reactions and 59% of patent reaction records use a transformation that the other side also performs. The shared core is small, simple chemistry, with a median of 3 changed atoms and 2 bond changes, against 7 and 6 for lab-only and 6 and 5 for enzyme-only transformations (L1x).

How large is the known space?

About 46,581 robust L1 transformations are documented in these two sources, and neither collection is close to complete.

Distinct L1 transformations as reactions are added

Random subsamples of each database

all transformationsseen in at least two reactions

US patents

Rhea

Table

In the last tenth of the patent data, each 100,000 extra reactions still add about 1,760 transformations seen at least twice (7,719 counting single sightings). In Rhea, each 1,000 extra reactions add about 72 (180). Extrapolating to a total (Chao1) is not meaningful for the patents, because atom-mapping errors inflate the single sightings that such estimates rely on.

How much has the lab achieved?

Almost all of the known space by count: 97% of the robust transformations come from the patents, which hold 96 times more reactions than Rhea. Reaction for reaction, the two are similarly diverse.

Distinct L1 transformations in US patents, by year of first appearance

Cumulative, all transformations

Table

The repertoire grows from 3,740 transformations in 1976 to 130,834 by 2016 without slowing down. Over the same years, the share of each year's patent reactions whose transformation enzymes also perform stays between 49% and 61%. Patent chemistry is concentrated. The 10 most frequent L1x transformations account for 31% of reaction records, the top 100 for 61% and the top 1,000 for 79%.

Where enzymes and labs differ

Share of each enzyme class's chemistry that the lab also does

L1, all transformations, by first EC digit

distinct transformationsreactions
Table

Lyases (26% of their transformations) and isomerases (29%) have the least lab precedent. These classes make and break C–C bonds, close rings and rearrange skeletons, the most enzyme-specific chemistry in the data.

The lab makes rings more often (44% of lab transformations form one, against 29% of enzymatic ones) and relies on elements and bond types that biology lacks: boron and tin for cross-coupling, silicon protecting groups, aryl halides, N–N bonds in new heteroaromatic rings. Enzymes are richer in phosphoryl transfer, metal-centred chemistry and changes of stereochemistry alone.

One transformation, several mechanisms

The same transformation is often reached in different ways. For enzymes, a mechanism label made of the EC sub-subclass and cofactors was checked against curated mechanisms in M-CSA. Enzyme pairs doing the same transformation have more similar mechanisms when they share the label (mean similarity 0.59 against 0.40; AUC 0.72). Of 4,195 such pairs, 3,664 have different curated mechanisms, so one transformation is often reached by several enzymatic routes.

Lab-only chemistry

"Lab only" means the transformation appears in the patents and in no Rhea reaction, in either direction. Rhea catalogues natural enzymes and their physiological reactions, so lab only does not rule out promiscuous, engineered or artificial enzymes; the literature check below looks for those. Has an enzyme done it anyway?

Rhea leaves out promiscuous, engineered and artificial enzymes. For the 500 most used lab-only transformations, grouped into chemistry families, Europe PMC was searched for enzymatic precedents. Each family got a verdict citing a paper that the search returned. The verdict also records what the catalyst needed beyond the 20 canonical amino acids and natural cofactors, which shows where natural side chains fall short.

Groups with a caveat (atom-mapping artefacts, mixed buckets, several steps in one record) hold 42% of these patent records. Without them, firm precedents cover 34% of the records and no precedent was found for 38%. For 13 of the families with no precedent (105,689 records), Rhea has an enzyme running the reverse reaction.

Verdicts are model judgements from titles and abstracts by ten annotators, then reviewed for consistency; the rules and every change are recorded in curated/README.md and in the verdict notes. Every cited DOI was found again by the recorded Europe PMC queries. The verdicts are a screen rather than a review, so check the paper before relying on one.

Beyond Rhea: what BRENDA adds

Rhea lists natural enzymes and their physiological reactions. BRENDA also records activity on other substrates, mostly the promiscuous activity of natural enzymes. Its reactions, atom-mapped and curated by EnzymeMap v2, went through the same pipeline: BRENDA reactions as reported, and reversed where BRENDA marks them reversible. Reactions with products that EnzymeMap inferred, and multi-step overall reactions, are left out.

Four enzyme sets against the lab

L1, all transformations; a reaction found in both databases is counted once

Enzyme setReactions TransformationsShared with the labLab transformations coveredPatent records covered
Rhea14,0823,6871,0070.8%59%
EnzymeMap37,3252,6097750.6%55%
EnzymeMap natural substrates7,9691,0854790.4%46%
Rhea + EnzymeMap48,7635,3581,2541.0%60%

BRENDA's 37,325 measured reactions add 1,704 L1x transformations that are in no Rhea reaction. Promiscuous activity is mostly the same transformation on other substrates, which the substrate-independent definition merges. EnzymeMap covers 228 of the 138,758 lab-only L1x transformations, 1.2% of their patent records.

Of the 500 most used lab-only transformations checked in the literature, 16 are in EnzymeMap. Checked by hand, 12 of these are coincidences between mis-mapped reactions (sulfate and CoA transfers, transaminations) and 4 are real chemistry:

  1. deoxyfluorination of alcohol to alkyl fluorideNo enzymatic precedent found in the literature check · sucrose phosphorylase run in reverse turns glucose 1-phosphate and fluoride into glucosyl fluoride: C-O to C-F at an anomeric carbon, missed by the literature screen
  2. Friedel-Crafts alkylation of arene with alkene (hydroarylation)Enzyme with parts nature lacks in the literature check · ThDP enzyme adds pyruvate to methyl vinyl ketone (Stetter-type conjugate addition): natural parts for the conjugate-addition part of this heterogeneous family
  3. thiol-Michael addition to activated alkeneNatural enzyme in the literature check · glutathione transferase adds glutathione to an acrylamide (thiol-Michael addition), consistent with the literature verdict
  4. SNAr alkoxylation of aryl fluorideNo enzymatic precedent found in the literature check · 4-fluorobenzoyl-CoA dehalogenase hydrolyses an aryl fluoride to the phenol; this signature of the family is hydrolysis, not alkoxylation

Literature biocatalysis: RetroBioCat

RetroBioCat curates synthetic biocatalysis from papers: which enzymes, wild type or engineered, convert which substrates, with negative results. Its records list the main substrates and the product but not cofactors or small co-substrates. The missing donors were added from the atom balance before mapping: water, ammonia, HCN, the methyl of a methylation, and the serine of tryptophan synthase. An incoming atom is described by its state in the product, so the choice of donor does not change the transformation.

The public sample: 2,924 positive results (of 3,653) from 68 papers. The full database is available from its authors on request; until then, what the sample finds is real and what it lacks says nothing.

The sample's 1,302 active reactions, 46 reaction types in all, reduce to 73 L1x transformations. 97% of the reactions use a transformation already in Rhea or EnzymeMap: synthetic biocatalysis mostly applies natural enzyme chemistry to new substrates, which the substrate-independent definition merges. 16 transformations are in neither database; 6 of them occur in patents.

2 are chemistry missing from both databases. 2 apply a Rhea transformation at two sites of one molecule. 7 are data-entry errors in RetroBioCat, such as an aldehyde drawn one carbon shorter than its acid. 5 are mis-mapped reactions. Errors and mis-mappings make transformations that no other reaction has. As with EnzymeMap, a match seen in a single reaction is weak evidence until it has been checked. The genuine ones cover 1,039 patent records; adding the sample to Rhea and EnzymeMap leaves the share of patent records with an enzymatic transformation at 56% (L1x).

Of the 500 most used lab-only transformations checked in the literature, the sample has 1:

  1. aldehyde to nitrile via aldoxime dehydration1,038 patent records · literature check: weak or partial precedent only, aldoxime dehydratase (Oxd, heme) · RetroBioCat: GOase M3-5, genuine · now cited in the verdict

Near misses: chemistry enzymes almost do

A lab-only transformation is a near miss when one named change turns it into something enzymes do. That change can be another reactant's point of view, another leaving group, one hydrogen more or fewer on one atom, or an aliphatic instead of an aromatic atom. The comparison edits the transformation's centre graph and looks it up among enzymatic transformations, using every reactant's point of view. Enzymatic neighbours count only if they are seen in at least two reactions, from Rhea in the physiological direction or from BRENDA as measured. Reverse matches are approximate and left out. Near misses are the first candidates for enzymes that should be possible: the chemistry exists in enzymes, one detail away.

The 30 most used near misses were checked by hand: 13 are genuine analogies, 9 are questionable (mostly sulfamate chemistry standing in for sulfonamides, which L1x cannot tell apart), 6 rest on mis-mapped enzyme reactions (Suzuki coupling's "near miss" is a transamination) and 2 could not be reproduced. The genuine ones:

  1. N-alkylation/N-arylation of amine (nucleophilic substitution)63,603 patent records · enzymes N-arylate a primary amine (isopropylamine onto a triazine, EC 3.5.4.42, a hydrolase annotated as reversible); the patents N-arylate secondary amines
  2. Knoevenagel condensation of active methylene with carbonyl14,759 patent records · an aldolase (EC 4.1.2.34) condenses a methyl ketone with an aldehyde to a C=C; the patents use an active methylene
  3. radical C(sp3)-H bromination10,338 patent records · flavin halogenases brominate aromatic C-H; the patents brominate methyl C-H
  4. organometallic addition to ketone (Grignard/organolithium)7,142 patent records · AIR carboxylase adds an aromatic C-H to CO2; the patents add an arene carbon (lithiated) to a ketone
  5. oxime formation from aldehyde3,319 patent records · oximinotransferase (EC 2.6.3.1) forms the oxime of a ketone (pyruvate) by oxime transfer; the patents form aldoximes
  6. alpha-bromination of ketone2,859 patent records · flavin halogenases brominate aromatic C-H; the patents brominate the alpha-CH2 of ketones
  7. organometallic addition to ketone (Grignard/organolithium)2,189 patent records · tryptophan synthase adds indole C3 to an aldehyde; the patents add a methyl organometallic
  8. C-C cross-coupling of organobromide1,821 patent records · prenyltransferases (EC 2.5.1.130) C-alkylate with diphosphate leaving from a CH2; the patents use alkyl bromides
  9. S-arylation of sulfinate to aryl sulfone1,177 patent records · sulfite adds to a CH2 (UDP-sulfoquinovose synthase); the patents S-arylate sulfinates
  10. C-C cross-coupling of organobromide1,011 patent records · indole prenyltransferases alkylate an arene with diphosphate leaving from a CH2; the patents use alkyl bromides
  11. SNAr amination of aryl chloride970 patent records · an amidase run in reverse makes an amide from an acid and ammonia; this signature of the family is acyl chloride amidation, not SNAr
  12. thiourea/urea formation from amine and isothiocyanate941 patent records · the same change from another reactant: ATP-dependent amide formation and cyclisation
  13. cyclic urea formation from diamine and urea913 patent records · dethiobiotin synthetase closes a cyclic urea from two primary amines and CO2; the patents use N-substituted diamines

How far to trust this

  • Lab means US patents. The lab set is the text-mined experimental sections of US patents, 1976–2016. Papers are missing because there is no large open dataset of reactions from the literature; Reaxys, CAS and Pistachio are commercial. Academic methods such as photoredox, electrochemistry and C–H functionalisation are under-represented.
  • Enzymes means Rhea, plus BRENDA. Rhea lists natural enzymes with a catalogued reaction; BRENDA (via EnzymeMap) adds measured activity on other substrates. Engineered and artificial enzymes are in neither, which the literature check addresses for the top lab-only chemistry. RetroBioCat's literature biocatalysis enters only as its public sample of 68 papers.
  • Atom mapping. RXNMapper and the patents' own atom maps give the same L1 signature for 76% of 19,998 sampled patent reactions (57% at the lowest mapping confidence, 92% at the highest). Mapping errors create spurious, mostly unique transformations, which is why the robust counts exist.
  • Robust filters change the distinct counts by a factor of two to three but leave the weighted shares unchanged, so the weighted shares are the most reliable numbers.
  • Representation limits. Ester hydrolysis is mapped as alkyl–oxygen cleavage, so it equals ether cleavage below L2. Amide coupling and acylation by an acid chloride are one transformation by design. A patent record can merge several steps. Rhea annotates the physiological direction for about half of its reactions; the others count in both directions.
